lead.t: •Lung volume reduction surgery (LVRS): peripheral emphysematous lung tissue is resected

snip.t: •Lung volume reduction surgery (LVRS): peripheral emphysematous lung tissue is resected

qs.q: A 65-year-old man with severe emphysema undergoes lung volume reduction surgery. Pathological examination of the resected tissue reveals destruction of the alveolar walls. What is the primary pathological definition of this condition?
o: Acute purulent exudate filling the alveolar spaces due to severe bacterial pneumonia
Reversible smooth muscle hypertrophy and goblet cell hyperplasia within the major bronchi
Fibrotic replacement of the terminal bronchioles accompanied by granulomatous inflammation
Permanent destructive enlargement of airspaces distal to terminal bronchioles without fibrosis
qs.e: Emphysema is defined pathologically as the permanent destructive enlargement of airspaces distal to the terminal bronchioles without obvious fibrosis. Fibrosis is not a primary feature of pure emphysema.

qs.q: What are the specific anatomical and physiological selection criteria for performing lung volume reduction surgery (LVRS)?
o: Predominantly lower lobe emphysema with severe pulmonary hypertension
Bilateral giant bullae formation with complete absence of lung tissue surrounding the lesions
Diffuse pan-acinar emphysema with an FEV1 and DLCO strictly below 10%
Predominantly upper lobe emphysema with preserved gas transference and no pulmonary hypertension
qs.e: Lung volume reduction surgery is indicated in patients with predominantly upper lobe emphysema who have preserved gas transference, no evidence of pulmonary hypertension, and FEV1 and DLCO values above 20%.

faq.a: Targeting the most diseased lobes yields the greatest reduction in hyperinflation and functional improvement.
faq.q: Why is LVRS offered only to patients with heterogeneous emphysema?

faq.a: Yes, if CD4 >200 cells/µL, viral load suppressed, and no active opportunistic infection.

exam: What physiologic parameters must be met before a patient is considered for LVRS? — FEV1 ≤45% predicted, TLC >100% predicted, DLCO >20% predicted, and heterogeneous upper‑lobe disease on CT.

A 58‑year‑old smoker with GOLD stage IV COPD worsens after bronchodilators. CT shows diffuse homogeneous emphysema. Would you recommend LVRS? — No, homogeneous disease predicts poor benefit; consider medical optimisation or lung transplantation.

During postoperative care, the patient develops a continuous air leak on day 5. What is your next step? — Maintain chest tube drainage, apply low‑pressure suction, and consider pleurodesis if leak persists beyond day 7.
How does LVRS improve diaphragmatic mechanics? — Resection reduces hyperinflation, allowing the diaphragm to assume a more domed shape, increasing its contractile efficiency.
Why are systemic steroids avoided in the peri‑operative period for LVRS? — They impair wound healing and increase infection risk, especially in low‑resource settings with limited sterility.

A patient with HIV presents with severe emphysema. What additional pre‑operative assessment is required? — CD4 count, viral load, and screening for opportunistic infections; ensure prophylaxis if CD4 <200.

Explain the difference between bullectomy and LVRS. — Bullectomy removes isolated bullae without addressing overall lung volume; LVRS removes a larger peripheral segment to reduce total lung capacity.
What postoperative complication mimics a pneumothorax on chest X‑ray and how to differentiate? — A large pleural effusion can appear radiolucent; ultrasound or CT can confirm fluid versus air.
ai.title: Lung Volume Reduction Surgery
ai.subject: Surgery
ai.summary: LVRS removes diseased peripheral emphysema to improve lung mechanics in selected severe COPD patients. It is offered after careful physiologic and radiologic assessment, especially where medical therapy fails.

b: Indicated for severe emphysema with heterogeneous disease distribution
Requires pre‑operative pulmonary function testing and high‑resolution CT
sections.p: Lung volume reduction surgery (LVRS) is a thoracic operation that resects the most emphysematous peripheral lung segments, reducing hyperinflation and improving diaphragmatic function.

b: GOLD stage III–IV (FEV1 ≤45% predicted)
Total lung capacity >100% predicted
Heterogeneous emphysema: upper‑lobe predominant disease with low‑attenuation areas >15% of lobe
sections.p: Patients are staged using GOLD criteria for COPD and the NETT (National Emphysema Treatment Trial) radiologic pattern.

b: Cigarette smoking
Indoor air pollution from wood/charcoal
HIV‑associated emphysema
Post‑tuberculosis bronchiectasis with emphysematous change
sections.p: LVRS is performed for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, most commonly due to tobacco smoking. In low‑resource East African settings, additional contributors include biomass fuel exposure and HIV‑related chronic lung disease.

b: Dyspnoea on minimal exertion (mMRC 3–4)
Use of accessory muscles
Decreased tactile fremitus over affected lobes
sections.p: Patients present with progressive dyspnoea, limited exercise tolerance, and a “barrel‑chest” appearance. Physical exam shows hyperinflated chest, flattened diaphragm, and reduced breath sounds over emphysematous zones.

t.b: Confirms airflow obstruction and quantifies severity; FEV1 ≤45% predicted supports LVRS candidacy
Identifies heterogeneous emphysema pattern and measures target lobe volume; if CT unavailable, use chest X‑ray with careful assessment of hyperinflation
Assesses gas exchange; DLCO >20% predicted is required for acceptable surgical risk
Detects chronic hypercapnia; PaCO2 >55 mmHg is a relative contraindication

b: Prolonged air leak >7 days
Post‑operative respiratory failure requiring ventilation
Bronchopleural fistula
Pneumothorax in contralateral lung
Pulmonary infection, especially in HIV/TB co‑infection
sections.p: Complications can be life‑threatening and require urgent attention.

b: Pre‑op bronchodilators (long‑acting β2‑agonist + inhaled anticholinergic) to reduce airway resistance
Smoking cessation ≥6 weeks before surgery
Pulmonary rehabilitation to improve functional reserve
Post‑op analgesia with epidural or paravertebral block to enable deep breathing
Early mobilisation and incentive spirometry
sections.p: LVRS is performed via video‑assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) or open thoracotomy after optimisation of medical therapy.

b: Clinic review at 2 weeks, 3 months, then 6 monthly
Repeat spirometry at 6 months to document FEV1 change
Vaccinations: influenza annually, pneumococcal per WHO schedule
Education on avoidance of indoor biomass smoke
sections.p: Long‑term benefit depends on continued smoking abstinence and rehabilitation.

b: Bullectomy – removal of isolated bullae without broader volume reduction
Lung transplantation – replaces diseased lung rather than resecting it
Bronchoscopic lung volume reduction (valves/coils) – endoscopic alternative
sections.p: Conditions that also reduce lung volume or mimic postoperative findings.

b: Normal chest X‑ray may miss heterogeneous emphysema; CT is essential
Spirometry alone cannot differentiate heterogeneous from homogeneous disease
ABG may show normal PaO2 at rest while exercise desaturation is severe
sections.p: Certain tests may appear reassuring despite high risk.

whenToSeekHelp: Chest pain with tachycardia suggesting pneumothorax
New fever and purulent sputum indicating infection
